threads.title: Build a portfolio someone can verify

posts.text: A Web3 portfolio needs a path from claim to evidence. For each project, show the problem, your contribution and something a reviewer can inspect. A title like 'growth lead' leaves all of that unanswered.

visual.headline: Make your work inspectable
visual.brief: Connect a project claim to a concrete artifact, with authorship marked between them.

posts.text: For an engineering sample, include a README with setup steps and tests for failure cases. Example: a withdrawal test should check what happens when the caller lacks permission, not only when the transfer succeeds.

visual.headline: Show the failure case
visual.brief: Compare two labeled test scenarios. This is a teaching diagram, not fabricated test output.

posts.text: For a marketing sample, write a campaign brief with an audience, a user action and a measurement plan. Example: a wallet tutorial can measure setup completion. Impressions alone won't tell you whether readers finished setup.

visual.headline: Connect content to an action
visual.brief: Map the proposed tutorial funnel without invented conversion rates.

posts.text: For community or operations work, show the system you built. A sample support runbook could explain how to collect an error report, assign an owner and tell the user when to expect an update.

visual.headline: Document a repeatable task
visual.brief: Draw a support ticket moving between user, moderator and engineer.

posts.text: Private work can still make a useful case study. Describe the constraint and your decision using approved, redacted material. Label a personal exercise as an exercise; don't turn it into a fictional client project.

visual.headline: Label the evidence honestly
visual.brief: Show three evidence formats with clear labels and no invented client identities.

posts.text: Before applying, open every portfolio link while logged out. Put the most relevant sample first, name your part in it and explain one limitation. A reviewer should be able to follow the evidence without requesting access.

visual.headline: Run the reviewer check
visual.brief: Use a compact pre-application checklist with one evidence link as the focal point.

supports.claims: Role-specific portfolios, runnable repositories, tests, documented nontechnical work, and accessible evidence links.
Authorship, confidentiality, accurate independent-work labels and logged-out link checks.

Q: What is signature replay, and how do you stop it?
A: Reusing a valid signed action. Sign and consume a nonce, bind the domain to chainId and verifyingContract, and enforce a deadline. EIP-712 alone does not prevent reuse.

items.title: AUD-I-02: Replay prevention
items.question: What is signature replay, and how do you stop it?
items.answer: Verify the signed action in the intended domain, require its current nonce, consume that nonce, and reject expired authorization.
facts: chainId and verifyingContract scope signatures to the intended chain and contract when included and verified.
A deadline limits validity time but does not make a message one-use before expiry.
EIP-712 standardizes signing; nonce consumption and action validation belong to the application.

Q: What is fuzzing, and which tool supports it?
A: Generated inputs search for broken properties. Echidna can fuzz call sequences; Foundry supports fuzz and invariant tests. Example for a simple custody vault: assets must cover recorded liabilities.

Q: Can an unbounded view loop cause denial of service?
A: Yes. eth_call still executes on an RPC node and can hit gas caps or timeouts. A getAllOwners() that grows forever can fail. Return bounded pages instead.

Off-chain reads consume node resources without paying a network transaction fee.
If the same computation is called inside a transaction, it also consumes transaction gas.

EIP-712 does not itself include replay protection. Domain fields include chainId and verifyingContract; applications must handle receiving the same signed message more than once.
A concrete signature authorization design includes the current owner nonce and deadline, increments the nonce after successful use, and uses a contract-and-chain-specific domain.

threads.title: Understand token approvals before signing

posts.text: An ERC-20 token approval gives another address permission to spend a specified token from your account. It is different from connecting a wallet to a website. Check the token, spender and amount before you approve.

visual.headline: Read the permission you are granting
visual.brief: Draw the relationship between token holder, token contract and approved spender. No real addresses.

posts.text: Example: you plan to swap 20 tokens, but the app requests an allowance of 200. That permission is larger than this trade. Where supported, set a cap that matches your intended use rather than accepting the requested amount automatically.

visual.headline: Compare the trade and the cap
visual.brief: Use two proportional bars labeled as a hypothetical token-quantity example, not prices.

posts.text: Disconnecting a website does not revoke an onchain token allowance. To remove that spending permission, submit a revocation on the relevant network and check that it confirms. An onchain revocation normally requires a network fee.

visual.headline: Disconnecting and revoking differ
visual.brief: Separate connection state from token-contract permission; show only revocation changing the allowance.

posts.text: A signature can authorize spending even when you pay no gas at signing. ERC-2612 permits let someone submit a signed approval onchain later. Read the spender, amount and deadline; a gasless prompt is not automatically a harmless login.

visual.headline: A signature can carry spending authority
visual.brief: Show signing followed by later onchain submission. Label the deadline as the permit submission deadline.

posts.text: NFT permissions use different scopes. setApprovalForAll can let an operator move every NFT you own from that collection contract. It is broader than approving one item, so check which collection and operator the request names.

visual.headline: Check the NFT permission scope
visual.brief: Compare single-item approval with all items under one collection contract, not all NFTs in a wallet.

posts.text: Review allowances by account and network, then remove ones you no longer need. Keep the approval and revocation receipts. Revoking permission cannot reverse a transfer that already happened, and it does not repair an exposed private key.

visual.headline: Keep an allowance review record
visual.brief: Show a permission inventory with no live balances. Distinguish permission cleanup from key compromise.

supports.claims: Token/spender/amount approval model, custom caps, collection-wide NFT operator approvals and limitations after assets are transferred.
Disconnecting differs from revocation, network-specific checks and onchain revocation gas fees.
Signed permits can be submitted by another address and include spender, value, nonce and deadline. The deadline limits permit submission, not the resulting allowance lifetime.
Private keys independently control accounts; permission revocation does not change a key.

A: Group fields that fit in 32 bytes. uint128, uint128, uint256 uses 2 slots; uint128, uint256, uint128 uses 3. Fewer slots do not guarantee cheaper writes.

posts.text:
Web3 Fundamentals (15 lessons): Wallets and Private Keys.
A wallet signs messages and transactions. In self-custody, you control keys or permissions; a custodian controls them for you. A signature proves account control, not legal identity.

visual.headline: Wallet control is not legal identity

items.title: Wallets and Private Keys
items.answer: Self-custody gives you control of keys or account permissions. Custodial services manage that control. Signatures establish account control.
facts: The course lists this as lesson 5, after Ethereum: The World Computer.
The lesson distinguishes displayed balances, account management and signing.
Wallet/account mechanisms vary; this does not assume every account is a single private key or has a seed phrase.

Decentralized Finance (9 lessons): Lending and Borrowing in DeFi.
Example: 80% LTV on $1,000 collateral gives an $800 borrowing cap. Liquidation uses a separate threshold, with parameters set per market.

items.title: Lending and Borrowing in DeFi
items.answer: Illustration: $1,000 collateral x 80% LTV = $800 borrowing cap. LTV and liquidation threshold are separate risk parameters.
facts: This lesson follows How Decentralized Exchanges (DEXs) Work.
The numbers are the lesson's hypothetical LTV example, not a current Aave or Compound quote.
Actual borrowing also depends on market liquidity, caps and asset configuration. Liquidation eligibility does not itself submit a liquidation transaction.

Web3 Marketing & Community (8 lessons): Growth Metrics and Analytics.
Unique Active Wallets counts addresses over a defined period. One person can control several. Retention asks how many wallets in a starting cohort return later.

items.title: Growth Metrics and Analytics
items.answer: Unique Active Wallets counts distinct active addresses in a period. Retention measures return activity from a defined starting cohort.
facts: One person can use multiple addresses, and one custodial address can represent multiple people.
Use the same cohort and return-action definitions when comparing periods.

AI x Crypto Intersection (7 lessons): Autonomous Agents.
Separate model, tools and wallet. Balance reads should not grant transfer-signing permission. Enforce spending caps and contract allowlists.

items.title: Autonomous Agents
items.answer: Separate model decisions, tool access and wallet signing. Grant permissions per action and enforce spending or contract restrictions.
facts: The lesson follows Introduction to AI x Crypto.
Its Trust and Guardrails section names spending caps, contract allowlists and approval thresholds.
The lesson recommends choosing permissions per action rather than automatically granting equal access to reads, drafts and transfer signing.

The live course contains 15 lessons and places Wallets and Private Keys fifth, after Ethereum: The World Computer.
Keys, addresses, and signatures explains wallet balances, account/key management, signing, self-custody versus custodial control, and signatures proving account control rather than legal identity.
Decentralized Finance contains nine lessons. Lending and Borrowing in DeFi is second, following How Decentralized Exchanges (DEXs) Work.

The lesson covers collateralized borrowing, asset/market-dependent LTV and liquidation thresholds. Its source quiz in content/learn/defi/lending.md supplies the hypothetical $1,000 at 80% LTV equals $800 example.

Aave lists Loan-to-Value and Liquidation Threshold as distinct borrow parameters, alongside asset availability and health factor. The thread's 80% example is not presented as a current Aave parameter.
Liquidation eligibility depends on health factor and collateral liquidation thresholds. A liquidator must submit a transaction; crossing a threshold is not autonomous scheduled execution.
Smart Contract Development contains nine lessons, with Testing Smart Contracts fifth after Smart Contract Security 101.

The actual Foundry example uses Solidity ^0.8.20, initializes 1,000 raw units, transfers 100, asserts recipient balance 100 and sender balance 900, and tests an insufficient-balance revert. The fuzz section varies bounded amounts. The source prerequisite is first-contract.
Forge supports Solidity assertions, generated-input fuzz tests, revert expectations and simulated callers. No fixed test count, speed guarantee or exhaustive input coverage is claimed.
Web3 Marketing & Community contains eight lessons; Growth Metrics and Analytics is lesson five.

Web3 Metrics Are Different distinguishes addresses from people. Unique Active Wallets counts distinct addresses; Retention uses returning wallet cohorts and consistent definitions. The source prerequisite is community.
AI x Crypto Intersection contains seven lessons. Autonomous Agents is second after Introduction to AI x Crypto.

How an Agent Works separates model, tools and wallet. Trust and Guardrails lists spending caps and contract allowlists and explicitly distinguishes balance reads, transaction drafts and transfer signing permissions.
